questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an increase in real output from broader development
questions.stem: A country's real output rises by 4 percent a year for a decade, while infant mortality, literacy and access to clean water all improve as well. Which statement best describes what has happened?

options.text: Output growth and development have occurred together, since development also covers health, education and living standards that the output figure omits
Only development has occurred, because a rising output total says nothing about how people live
options.misconception: treats real output growth as evidence that nothing improved

options.text: Only output growth has occurred, because gains in health and education are not economic outcomes
options.misconception: denies that health and education count as economic outcomes

options.text: Neither has occurred, since a decade is too short a period to count as growth
options.misconception: requires an arbitrarily long period before growth is real

questions.explanation: Development is the broader claim: it covers material output and also the distribution of income, the quality of public services, health and education. A rising real total is necessary for sustained development but does not establish it, since the same average output can coexist with a widening gap or with falling life expectancy. Treating the output figure as the whole story ignores what the extra output is being spent on, and dismissing the service gains mistakes development for a purely material measure.
questions.hint: Ask what else the extra output is being converted into.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: define economic growth as an increase in real output
questions.stem: A country's real gross domestic product rises from 1,000 billion to 1,050 billion currency units over one year while the deflator is unchanged at 100. What does this movement record?

options.text: Economic growth, because the quantity of final output produced has risen at constant prices
No growth, because the deflator stayed the same and so nothing has been revalued
options.misconception: believes a constant deflator rules out any real change

options.text: Pure inflation, because a larger nominal total can only come from higher prices
options.misconception: labels every rise in output as a price-level effect

options.text: Population growth, because a bigger total requires more people to produce it
options.misconception: assumes a larger real total cannot come from better productivity

questions.explanation: Economic growth is a rise in the quantity of final output, measured at constant prices so that a change in the price level is not counted as production. With the deflator at 100 in both years the real total is 1,000 and then 1,050 billion, a gain of 5 percent of physical output. A stable deflator is exactly what makes this reading possible, so treating it as evidence of no change reverses the role of the deflator, and calling the movement inflation requires prices to have risen when they did not.
questions.hint: A constant deflator means both years are priced the same way.

questions.learningObjective: compute the effect of a sustained growth rate on the level of output
questions.stem: An economy's real output is 500 billion units today and grows at a constant 5 percent a year. Ignoring any change in population, what is the level of real output after four years of that growth?

600.00 billion units, because 5 percent of 500 is 25 a year for four years
options.misconception: adds the growth each year instead of compounding it

options.text: 520.00 billion units, because only the first year's increase carries into the total
options.misconception: counts a single year's gain and ignores the following three

options.text: 625.00 billion units, because a constant rate adds a quarter of the original output each year
options.misconception: compounds at a rate applied to the starting level every year

questions.learningObjective: use the rule of seventy to estimate the doubling time of output
questions.stem: A country's real output per person is rising at 2.5 percent a year and the rate is expected to hold. Roughly how many years will it take for the figure to double?

About 40 years, because the rate has to be halved before doubling can begin
options.misconception: halves the growth rate instead of dividing 70 by it

options.text: About 2.5 years, because 70 times the rate gives the number of years
options.misconception: multiplies 70 by the rate rather than dividing

options.text: About 25 years, because a doubling always takes exactly 100 divided by 4 percent
options.misconception: borrows the answer for a four percent rate and ignores the stated one

The exact figure from 1.025 raised to the power of 28 is 1.9994, which is almost exactly a doubling, so the rule is a good approximation here. Halving the rate, multiplying 70 by the rate, or importing the number for a different rate all produce a figure the rule does not produce.
questions.hint: The rule is a division, with the rate written as a plain percentage number.

questions.learningObjective: identify the denominator of a per capita measure
questions.stem: A report announces that average output per person has risen from 3,000 to 3,300 units over five years. Which quantity sits in the denominator of that measure?

options.misconception: divides by workers rather than by the whole population

options.text: The adult population, because children do not consume the output produced
options.misconception: restricts the denominator to adults and so overstates the average

options.text: Total output, because the average is that total expressed against itself
options.misconception: divides total output by total output and so gets one

questions.explanation: A per capita figure divides an aggregate by the number of people living in the economy, so 3,000 and 3,300 are total real output over population. The denominator is the whole resident population because the standard of living applies to every resident, not only to producers or only to adults. Dividing by the labour force measures output per worker, a different and higher number that answers a different question, and dividing by total output yields a ratio of one by construction.
questions.hint: Ask how many people the standard of living is averaged over.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain catch-up growth and the convergence debate
questions.stem: A poor country with output per person of 8,000 units grows at 4 percent a year while a rich country at 40,000 grows at 1 percent. What does the theory of catch-up predict?

options.text: The gap narrows over time, because a low capital stock per worker makes extra investment more productive
The gap widens, because rich countries can always afford more capital per worker
options.misconception: assumes the rich country's higher saving guarantees a faster catch-up

options.text: The gap is fixed forever, because growth rates never converge across countries
options.misconception: holds that technology differences are permanent and never shrink

options.text: The two converge at once, because richer countries must slow to the poorest country's pace
options.misconception: assumes the rich country must match the poor country's rate exactly

questions.explanation: In a model with diminishing returns to capital, a country that begins with little capital per worker can expect a high return on the next unit of capital, so extra saving translates into faster output growth until capital per worker approaches the frontier. The gap between 8,000 and 40,000 therefore narrows rather than widens. Wealth alone does not determine the pace of catch-up, and the two rates need not become identical: the poor country can keep growing faster while the gap closes, and any gap traced to technology rather than capital will not close on its own.
questions.hint: Diminishing returns make extra capital more valuable where there is little of it.

questions.learningObjective: link a country's saving rate to the investment it finances
questions.stem: In a closed economy with no government, national saving is 240 billion units and gross investment is 240 billion. What does this identity say about who finances investment?

options.text: Domestic saving finances all of it, because in a closed economy without government, saving must equal investment
Foreign lenders finance it, because investment normally exceeds domestic saving
options.misconception: assumes investment must be financed from abroad in a closed economy

options.text: The government finances it, because only the public sector can borrow for investment
options.misconception: credits the government in an economy specified to have none

options.text: Nobody finances it, because 240 billion of saving is too small to fund 240 billion
options.misconception: believes saving and investment must differ in magnitude

questions.hint: In a closed economy with no government, the two totals must be the same number.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state the golden rule condition for the capital stock
questions.stem: In a Solow model, the golden rule capital stock is defined as the stock that maximises consumption per worker in the long run. Which condition identifies it?

options.text: The marginal product of capital equals the sum of population growth and depreciation
The marginal product of capital equals population growth alone, ignoring wear
options.misconception: omits the depreciation term from the break-even requirement

options.text: The average product of capital equals population growth plus depreciation
options.misconception: uses the average product of capital instead of the marginal one

options.text: The marginal product of capital equals the rate of return net of depreciation
options.misconception: sets the gross marginal product against the real rate of return

questions.explanation: Consumption per worker is f(k) less (n plus delta)k, so its maximum is where the extra output from one more unit of capital exactly offsets the extra capital needed per person and the wear on that unit, which is d(c per worker)/dk = f'(k) minus n minus delta = 0. The condition is f'(k) = n + delta. Using the average product or the net return replaces the marginal product that governs the next unit of investment with a quantity that averages over the whole stock.
questions.hint: Set the derivative of consumption per worker equal to zero.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: characterise the Solow steady state
questions.stem: In the Solow model, the capital stock per worker stops growing when investment exactly replaces the capital needed to equip new workers and the capital that wears out. What is this condition called?

options.text: The steady state, where capital per worker is constant and output per worker grows only with technology
The golden rule, where the marginal product of capital is at its maximum
options.misconception: confuses the steady state with the consumption-maximising stock

options.text: A poverty trap, where the capital stock per worker is fixed and cannot rise
options.misconception: reads a constant capital stock as an inability to accumulate

options.text: A convergence club, where countries share one common growth rate
options.misconception: borrows a term from cross-country growth accounting

questions.explanation: The steady state is the point at which gross investment per worker is exactly sufficient to cover population dilution and depreciation, so the capital stock per worker is constant while output per worker is constant too in the version without technological progress. It is a fixed level, not a fixed rate, so describing it as an inability to grow mistakes a long-run level for a short-run performance. The golden rule is a different point on the same path, chosen to maximise consumption rather than to stop growth.
questions.hint: A constant capital stock per worker is a level, not a growth rate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain diminishing returns to capital in the growth model
questions.stem: A country keeps adding to its capital stock per worker while its technology and its labour force are unchanged. What happens to the extra output generated by each further unit of capital?

options.text: It falls, because a fixed labour force spreads itself over more and more capital
It rises, because a larger capital stock attracts a larger labour force
options.misconception: lets the labour force grow with the capital stock and hold it fixed

options.text: It stays constant, because extra capital is matched one for one by extra output
options.misconception: assumes constant returns to capital rather than diminishing ones

options.text: It falls to zero at once, because capital adds nothing beyond the first unit
options.misconception: treats diminishing returns as if they reached zero immediately

questions.explanation: With the labour force fixed, each additional unit of capital has a smaller labour force to work with, so the marginal product of capital falls: f'(k) declines as k rises. This is the mechanism that produces a steady state, because investment must eventually be large enough merely to offset the shrinking return. Returns do not vanish, they just decline, and a larger capital stock does not enlarge the labour force, so it cannot restore the return to its earlier level.
questions.hint: The labour force is not growing, so more capital means less capital per worker.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify technological progress as the source of sustained per capita growth
questions.stem: In a Solow model with a fixed saving rate and a fixed labour force, output per worker stops growing once the steady state is reached. What single change allows growth per worker to continue indefinitely?

options.text: A continuing increase in total factor productivity, which raises what each unit of input can produce
A one-off rise in the saving rate, which lifts the steady-state capital stock
options.misconception: expects a single saving change to sustain growth forever

options.text: A one-off rise in the capital stock, which can then be grown into
options.misconception: treats a level shift in capital as a permanent growth engine

options.text: A faster rate of population growth, which raises the number of workers
options.misconception: counts a rising headcount as higher output per person

questions.explanation: With a fixed saving rate, a fixed labour force and no productivity change, diminishing returns drive capital per worker to a fixed level and output per worker stops growing. Only a continuing rise in total factor productivity changes the production function itself, raising the steady-state level and permitting growth per worker to persist, and it can do so indefinitely because there is no natural limit to how much better the production process can become. A one-off change in the saving rate moves the economy to a higher fixed level, and more workers raise total output without raising output per person.
questions.hint: Ask which change alters the production function rather than the quantity of one input.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: define a shift in total factor productivity
questions.stem: Output rises 5 percent in one year while both the capital stock and the labour force are unchanged. What does that pattern indicate about the production function?

options.text: A positive total factor productivity shock, because output rose with no change in either measured input
Faster labour force growth, since more output came from employing more workers
options.misconception: attributes the whole rise to a change in measured labour

options.text: Faster capital accumulation, since output rose while both inputs held still
options.misconception: attributes the whole rise to a change in measured capital

options.text: A fall in the capital share of income, since extra output came from nowhere
options.misconception: explains higher output by changing the exponent on capital

questions.explanation: Total factor productivity is the residual in the production function, the part of output not explained by the measured inputs. If output rises while the capital stock and the labour force do not move, the only place left is the efficiency with which those inputs are combined, so the shock is unambiguously positive. Attributing it to a change in either input contradicts the premise that both were unchanged, and shifting a share of income would change how output is divided rather than how much is produced from a given input.
questions.hint: Both measured inputs are stated to be unchanged, so the change must be in efficiency.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: describe the membership problem of a convergence club
questions.stem: A convergence club is defined as the set of countries whose income levels per person were similar when growth data were first collected. What difficulty does that definition create?

options.text: Membership depends on an arbitrary cut-off year, so countries can be inside or outside the club purely by where they happened to be
Membership is impossible to compute, because income per person is never observed directly
options.misconception: treats the membership variable as unobservable when it is measured

options.text: Membership is fixed forever, so later growth rates cannot change the grouping
options.misconception: holds the initial grouping immune to subsequent growth

options.text: Membership requires identical technology, which is never true of any two countries
options.misconception: requires technology identity rather than similar starting income

questions.explanation: The club is defined by initial income, and the cut-off is a convention rather than a fact of the data, so a country near the boundary can be classified either way without any economic change having occurred. Membership does not stay fixed in the sense of excluding later evidence, and it is not defined by anything as strong as identical technology.
questions.hint: The grouping is decided by an initial level, and levels near the cut-off sit on a knife edge.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: describe how a terms-of-trade shock is transmitted to a country
questions.stem: The world price of oil falls by a third while a country is a net oil exporter. Which chain of events carries that fall into its national income?

options.text: Export revenue in domestic currency falls, so national income falls by the lost export earnings and by the higher cost of oil it still imports
Export revenue rises, because cheaper oil increases the volume a country can sell abroad
options.misconception: reads a lower price as a rise in the value of exports

options.text: Domestic oil production rises, because a lower price stimulates drilling of new wells
options.misconception: claims a price fall increases the quantity produced domestically

options.text: The trade balance is unaffected, because only the quantity of oil trades internationally
options.misconception: believes the value of trade is independent of the price

questions.explanation: The terms of trade is the price of exports relative to the price of imports, so a third off the price of oil cuts the domestic-currency value of oil exports by roughly a third on the exported volume. A net exporter therefore loses export income, and any oil it still buys for its own use becomes more expensive, so the national income loss is the sum of the two effects. A lower price does not add to export value on its own and does not by itself stimulate new domestic supply, since the incentive runs the other way.
questions.hint: A net exporter earns less when the world price of its export falls.

questions.learningObjective: explain how a debt overhang reduces investment
questions.stem: A government owes 60 percent of a year's output at an interest rate of 8 percent a year, so debt service takes 21.8 percent of revenue. How does that position depress investment?

options.text: Debt service crowds out the government's capacity to finance public investment, and the risk of default raises the interest rate private firms must pay
Debt service raises investment, because lenders prefer an economy with more public capital
options.misconception: treats a heavy debt burden as a spur to public capital formation

options.text: Debt service crowds out consumption only, leaving investment free to expand
options.misconception: confines the crowding out to private consumption

options.text: Debt service has no effect, because 21.8 percent of revenue is a small enough share
options.misconception: assumes a fifth of revenue leaves scope for unlimited investment

Neither channel is a statement about consumption, and a fifth of revenue is not a rounding error: it is a large claim on every year's budget.

questions.learningObjective: identify the cause of capital flight
questions.stem: Residents of a country move their savings abroad, and the exchange rate is expected to fall by a quarter next year. What is the direct cause of that outflow?

A rise in domestic saving, which necessarily flows straight out of the country
options.misconception: treats a rise in national saving as an outflow by definition

options.text: A shortage of foreign currency, which forces residents to hold only domestic assets
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the flow in the presence of a shortage

options.text: A ban on foreign investment, which is the usual trigger for the outflow
options.misconception: treats a capital-control law as the usual cause of flight

questions.learningObjective: name the specific institution that the institutions argument turns on
questions.stem: The institutions argument holds that two countries with the same resources grow at different rates because of how they are governed. Which specific institution does it emphasise?

questions.learningObjective: identify the two channels of a resource curse
questions.stem: A country with abundant oil grows more slowly per person than a resource-poor neighbour. Which two channels does the resource curse run through?

questions.learningObjective: explain the mechanism of Dutch disease
questions.stem: A sudden oil boom in a small open economy drives up demand for its non-traded services, and construction wages rise faster than output per worker in the whole economy. What does that do to the traded sector?

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.topic: Growth claim contradicted by a per capita series
questions.learningObjective: explain why a per capita series can refute a claim of growth
questions.stem: A government reports that its economy grew by 4 percent each year for five years. A demographer reports that the population grew by 6 percent each year over the same five years. Explain why the per capita series contradicts the government's claim.

answer.exemplar: Real output per person is the ratio of the two, so it changes by 1.04 divided by 1.06 in each year, which is 0.98113, a fall of about 1.9 percent a year and roughly 9 percent over the five years. The claim of growth refers to the total, which did rise by 4 percent a year, but living standards are measured per person, and with the population growing faster than output each person's share of the total falls every year. Both statements can be literally true at once, so the contradiction is not a matter of arithmetic but of which measure the word growth is being used for. If the intended claim was about living standards, it is false; if it was deliberately about aggregate output, the per capita series simply answers a different question and the headline is misleading rather than wrong.

questions.explanation: Divide the two growth factors; a ratio falls when the denominator grows faster.
questions.hint: Both reports can be true at the same time, so nothing here is arithmetically wrong: output per person is a ratio, and a ratio falls when the denominator grows faster than the numerator, which is exactly what 6 percent against 4 percent produces. The trap is that the word growth has come to mean an improvement in living standards, and a 4 percent rise in a total divided among 6 percent more people is a deterioration for every additional person. Concluding that output and population both rose, so per person is fine, compares a nominal total with a headcount and never removes the price effect at all.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: define an inclusive institution and state its effect on the steady state
questions.stem: Two countries have the same resources, the same technology and the same saving rate, but one holds elections in which governments can be replaced and the other does not. Explain what the difference does to long-run output per worker in each country.

answer.exemplar: The country that can replace its governments is the one with inclusive institutions: political power is contestable, so the returns to investment, taxation and effort are spread across many people rather than captured by a narrow group. The consequence is that more of the return to any given project accrues to the person who made it, so private saving and investment are higher, the Solow steady-state capital stock per worker is higher, and output per worker settles at a higher level even though the saving rate and the technology are given as identical. In the country without contestable power, effort is diverted into securing rents, the capital stock stops growing sooner, and the same resources produce less. Note what is not doing the work here: the difference is not a higher natural endowment or a better technology but the distribution of the return to effort, which is what an inclusive institution changes.

questions.explanation: Ask who gets the return when a project succeeds in each country.
questions.hint: Once the saving rate and the technology are held fixed, the steady-state capital stock is pinned down by the production function, so the only way two economies with identical resources can end at different levels of output per worker is if something in the return to effort differs between them. Contestable political power is that something: where a government can be replaced, the gain from a successful investment is more likely to reach the person who made it, which is exactly what a private owner needs in order to fund it. Claiming the difference must lie in natural resources or in the discovery of better technology runs into the premise that both are the same, and it also leaves unexplained why a country with plenty of both can still be poor.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a low initial capital stock can persist as a low growth rate
questions.stem: Two economies are identical in every respect except that one began with a capital stock per worker of 4 and the other with 40, and both have the same saving rate, technology and rate of depreciation. Explain how the difference can persist for many decades.

answer.exemplar: Both economies are heading to the same steady state, so the economy that began at 4 must grow faster for as long as the gap lasts, because each unit of investment buys more output when it is added to a small stock where the marginal product of capital is high. That is the optimistic reading, and it is why the initial condition is usually described as temporary. The reason the gap can persist anyway is that the adjustment is slow: with population growth and depreciation together taking a fixed share of output, the convergence path from 4 to 64 is asymptotic, so the level gap narrows in percentage terms while remaining large in absolute terms for decades. Persistence is made worse whenever the mechanism that would lift the low-capital economy works only slowly, for example when the constraint that kept capital low is a credit constraint that is relaxed gradually, or when the technology that determines the steady state is itself slow to diffuse from the leading country.

questions.explanation: Compare the marginal product of capital at the two starting stocks, then ask how long closing the gap takes.
questions.hint: The two economies have the same steady state, so the difference between them is a gap to be closed rather than a different destination, and the closing is driven by the higher marginal product of capital at the low starting stock. What makes the gap durable is the speed of the adjustment: break-even investment takes a fixed share of output every year, so the approach to the steady state is asymptotic and the level gap stays large for decades even while the ratio narrows. A story in which the two grow at the same rate forever is a story about the technology or the steady state differing, which the premise rules out, and a story in which the gap vanishes in a few years ignores how slowly a capital stock is built relative to the income being spent on it.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain both channels of a resource curse
questions.stem: A country discovers oil and begins exporting it. Twenty years later its real income per person is lower than in a country that never had oil. Explain the two channels through which the discovery can produce that outcome.

answer.exemplar: The first channel runs through the real exchange rate. An export boom bids up wages and the price of non-traded services, because the demand for those services comes from the income the oil sector is generating, while the nominal exchange rate is pinned by tradable prices. Domestic costs therefore rise faster than foreign prices, the currency appreciates in real terms, and tradable manufacturing is crowded out by imports; the country ends up more dependent on a volatile primary product and no better off per person. The second channel runs through politics. A large and concentrated stream of oil rent gives groups inside the country an incentive to compete for its division rather than to create new output, so talented people move into lobbying, into the public sector and into rent extraction, and the return to productive activity falls. The two channels reinforce each other, because a weaker tradable sector makes the economy more dependent on the volatile price and a more dependent economy gives rent-seeking more to fight over.

questions.explanation: Two channels: one moves the real exchange rate, the other moves effort away from production.
questions.hint: Each channel is a distinct failure, and the trap is to think that finding one of them is enough. The real exchange rate channel says the tradable sector shrinks, which is a claim about composition: the country can be just as busy and earn the same oil income while producing less that can be traded. The political channel says the return to creating output falls, which is a claim about effort, and it applies to a country whose oil income is unchanged. Attributing the whole outcome to the exchange rate leaves the incentives unexamined, and attributing it to corruption alone leaves the currency and the tradables out of the story, which is why the two have to be named separately.
